question: What sits between every program and the physical hardware of a computer?
correct: The operating system
incorrect: The web browser currently running
The network card and its cable
The programming language the code was written in
feedback: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS all play the same role. A useful picture: the OS is the building manager and programs are tenants — tenants never wire their own electricity.

question: Match each operating-system job to what it involves.

pairs.definition: Starting and stopping programs, and slicing CPU time between them
Organising the disk into named files and folders
Giving each program its own protected slice of RAM

feedback: These three jobs are why dozens of programs appear to run at once, why no program needs to know where bits physically live, and why a buggy game cannot scribble over your documents.

question: What is a process?
correct: One running program, managed by the operating system
incorrect: A single function inside a larger program
A file stored on disk waiting to be opened
A step in the fetch-decode-execute cycle
feedback: The OS starts processes, schedules them, and stops them. Your notebook itself appears in the machine's process table as a python3 process — one tenant among many.

question: Why does one crashing app usually not take down the whole machine?
correct: The OS gives each process protected memory and mediates hardware access
incorrect: Modern apps are written so carefully that crashes stay local
Each app runs on a separate processor core of its own
The hardware detects the crash and restarts that app
feedback: Programs ask the OS for what they need rather than commanding the hardware, and the OS decides. That mediation is the protection.

question: What does DNS do?
correct: Translates a name such as python.org into an IP address
incorrect: Splits a message into packets and numbers them
Encrypts a request so nobody can read it in transit
Chooses which of a company's servers has the least load
feedback: The rule is that you cannot deliver to a name, only to an address. DNS is the internet's phone book, consulted millions of times a second before any real conversation begins.

question: Looking up the same big website twice can return different IP addresses. Why?
correct: Large sites run many machines behind one name, and DNS shares them out
incorrect: The address changes each time a page on the site is edited
DNS invents an address when the real one is unavailable
Each user is permanently assigned their own copy of the site
feedback: DNS acts like a receptionist directing a queue. It is also why a stale or wrong DNS entry can make a site vanish for one region while everyone else sees nothing wrong.

question: How does a message actually travel across the internet?
correct: It is chopped into numbered packets that each find their own way
incorrect: It travels whole along a single reserved wire to the destination
It is copied to each machine on the network until one accepts
It is stored on a central internet server that the receiver checks
feedback: Packets hop router to router, can arrive out of order, and some do not arrive at all. That is the problem the next layer has to solve.

question: What does TCP add on top of packets?
correct: Numbering, confirmation, re-sending, and reassembly in order
incorrect: The name-to-address lookup before the message is sent
Encryption of the contents so they are unreadable
The rule that the largest packets are delivered first
feedback: It works like a parcel-tracking system: number every parcel, confirm each arrival, re-send anything unconfirmed, and reassemble in order. The message arrives complete, or the sender knows it did not.

question: Match each layer of the TCP/IP model to its one job.

pairs.definition: What the messages mean — HTTP, DNS
The physical hop — Wi-Fi, cable, fibre

feedback: Each layer talks only to the ones directly above and below it. That is why engineers could replace copper with fibre and then with 5G without anything above the link layer noticing.

question: Why is the layered design of the TCP/IP model so useful?
correct: An entire layer can be replaced without the layers above it needing to change
incorrect: It lets a message skip layers when the network is busy
It guarantees that no packet is ever lost in transit
It means four programs are enough to run the whole internet
feedback: HTTP never worries about lost packets; that is transport's job. TCP never worries about which cable to use; that is the link layer's job. It is the same trick an operating system plays, stacked four layers high.

question: An HTTP conversation has exactly two turns. What are they?
correct: A request naming a verb and an address, and a response with a status code
incorrect: A name lookup and then a packet transfer
A login and then a download of the whole site
A question from the server and an answer from the browser
feedback: The usual verb is GET, meaning please send me. The response carries the content plus a three-digit verdict describing how it went.

question: Match each HTTP status code to what it means.

pairs.definition: Moved permanently — here is the new address
Not found — no such thing at this address
Server error — the server failed while answering

feedback: A good HTTP conversation fails informatively. A diagnostician learns as much from a 404 as from a 200, because the server answered rather than going silent.

question: A request is sent for a page that does not exist, and the program receives a 404 without crashing. What does this show?
correct: The server answered normally; the code is the report that it is missing
incorrect: The request failed to reach the server
The network dropped the packets on the way back
The client library failed to parse the response
feedback: No crash and no silence — just a calm verdict meaning that is not a thing. Status codes are how HTTP reports failure as data rather than as an accident.

question: What is an API, as the term is used here?
correct: A server whose job is answering programs rather than showing pages
incorrect: A library of functions that comes built into Python
The part of a website a human clicks through
A password that lets a program connect to a network
feedback: An app that needs weather does not scrape it off a web page; it asks an API and gets clean JSON back. Most modern software is programs having HTTP conversations with other programs.

question: Why does an API usually answer in JSON rather than in HTML?
correct: JSON is labelled data a program turns straight into dictionaries
incorrect: JSON transmits across the network faster than any other format
HTML is unsuitable as the body of an HTTP response
JSON is encrypted while HTML is sent as plain text
feedback: HTML is for showing things to people; JSON is for handing data to programs. The response converts directly into the Python data structures you already know how to work with.

question: What are HTTP headers?
correct: Labelled notes on the outside of a message, such as Content-Type
incorrect: The first few lines of the page's visible content
The list of packets that make up the message
The section of a web page holding its title and menus
feedback: Think of writing on an envelope. Content-Type tells the receiver how to read the body — application/json means parse me as JSON — and much of the web's hidden machinery, including logins and caching, lives in headers.

question: How is "the cloud" defined in this notebook?
correct: Someone else's computer, rented by the slice and reachable over the network
incorrect: A network of machines with no single physical location
Storage that is duplicated across each user's device
Software that runs wholly inside the web browser
feedback: The only interesting question is how big a slice you rent — which is exactly what the three service models answer.

question: Match each cloud service model to the housing analogy for it.

pairs.definition: Renting bare land — you manage the OS and everything above it
Renting an apartment — you bring only your code
Booking a hotel room — you just use finished software

feedback: Amazon EC2 is IaaS, Heroku and App Engine are PaaS, and Gmail is SaaS. The more the landlord manages, the less control and less responsibility you have.

question: Which of these are true of Google Colab, in cloud terms? (Select all that apply)
correct: It is finished software used through a browser, which is SaaS
It hands you a managed Linux machine to run code on
incorrect: It gives you bare virtual machines needing an OS installed
It runs wholly on your own computer, with no server involved
feedback: You have been a cloud customer all semester. The Linux box whose processes you can list is a slice of someone else's computer.

question: Stripped of mystique, what is a web server?
correct: A program that waits, running some code and returning a response for each request
incorrect: A specialised computer built for hosting websites
A folder of HTML files that a browser downloads directly
The part of the operating system that handles the network card
feedback: It is a process — a tenant of some operating system, like every other program. That is why the fastest way to understand one is to become one.

question: In Flask, what does a route do?
correct: Pairs a path such as /status with the function that answers requests for it
incorrect: Chooses which router the response packets travel through
Redirects a visitor from one website to another
Decides which port number the server should listen on
feedback: The decorator line above a function declares: when a request arrives for this path, run this function and send back whatever it returns.

question: What does the placeholder in the route  /tip/<int:tip_id>  accomplish?
correct: It captures the number from the address and passes it to the function
incorrect: It restricts the route to administrators of the site
It creates a separate route for each possible tip number
It converts the whole page into an integer before sending it
feedback: Visiting /tip/2 hands the function tip_id = 2 as a real Python int. That is how one route answers differently depending on what the visitor asked for.

question: A Flask route ends with  return page, 404. What does the second value do?
correct: It sets the HTTP status code of the response
incorrect: It limits the page to 404 characters in length
It retries the request 404 milliseconds later
It records the number of visitors the route has had
feedback: The page explains the problem to a human and the code reports it to a program. That is a server failing informatively, exactly like the well-behaved APIs questioned earlier.

question: The notebook says most web pages do not exist until you ask for them. What does that mean?
correct: A function builds the HTML on the spot from data, and returns it as a string
incorrect: Pages are stored as files but deleted after each visitor leaves
Pages are assembled inside the browser from data it already had
Pages exist just while a database query is still running
feedback: There is no file anywhere holding your social feed or your bank statement page. A page is just a string a server computed — and you already know how to compute strings.

question: Which of these are jobs the operating system does for a running program? (Select all that apply)
correct: Deciding when it gets a slice of CPU time
Granting and later reclaiming its memory
Locating a file on disk when it asks to open one
incorrect: Checking that its logic produces correct results
Translating its Python source into a different language
feedback: The OS manages resources; it makes no judgement about whether your code is right. Every byte your variables occupy was granted by the OS and is reclaimed when the process ends.

question: A streaming site is down in one city but fine in another, and down at busy times but fine at quiet ones. Investigation found one of three server processes had crashed days earlier with nothing restarting it. Why does that explain the pattern?
correct: Requests routed to the dead process vanished, more often when busy
incorrect: A crashed process makes DNS return the wrong address in nearby regions
The remaining processes ran more slowly because one was missing
TCP stopped confirming packets once a server process ended
feedback: Two survivors coped most of the time, so the failure looked random and regional. Listing the machine's processes — the very first tool in the notebook — would have shown a corpse in the table.

question: Which sequence correctly describes one full request to a website?
correct: Name lookup, request in packets, server process runs, response in packets, page rendered
incorrect: Request in packets, name lookup, page rendered, server process runs
Server process runs, name lookup, response in packets, request in packets
Page rendered, request in packets, name lookup, server process runs
feedback: The name lookup happens before the real request. After that, the request and response each cross the network as packets that TCP reassembles at either end.

question: The numeric address that identifies one machine on a network is called an ___ address.
correct: IP
feedback: IP stands for Internet Protocol. Numbers, not names, are what the network actually routes — which is why DNS has to translate first.

question: In HTML, the piece of markup that wraps text to say what it is, such as the h1 or p pair, is called a ___.
correct: tag
feedback: Tags almost always come in an open and close pair, with the closing one carrying a slash. A page is just a string with a few of them in it.

question: Which of these are reasons a company might choose SaaS over IaaS? (Select all that apply)
correct: Nobody on the team has to manage an operating system or servers
The software is ready to use immediately through a browser
incorrect: It gives the most control over exactly how the machines are configured
It is the model that keeps data on the company's own hardware
It removes the need for any network connection
feedback: SaaS trades control for convenience: you are a user, and nothing underneath is your problem. IaaS is the opposite trade — total control and total responsibility.
